items.title: The Post-Mauryan Period & Political Landscape
items.body:
## The Post-Mauryan Period & Political Landscape

**In one line:** The post-Mauryan period is the gap between the fall of the Mauryas and the rise of the Guptas, when regional Indian dynasties (Shungas, Kanvas, Chedis) ruled while Central Asian peoples invaded the north-west.

**Why it is asked:** Examiners test the "which dynasties filled the gap" idea and the sequence of foreign invaders, so a clear overview anchors every other note in this topic.

### The story
- **Cause:** the Mauryan Empire **disintegrated after Ashoka's death** under weak successors, and provinces began **declaring independence**.
- **What happened:** the period (**2nd century BCE – 3rd century AD**) saw **regional kingdoms** rise — the **Shungas, Kanvas and Chedis** — while the **north-west** was invaded in turn by the **Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Parthians and Kushanas**.
- **Result:** **Kalinga became independent**, the **Satavahanas** took the south, and the **Shungas, followers of Brahmanism**, replaced the Mauryas and reacted against their Buddhist policy.

### Picture it
```
Mauryas ──▶ [POST-MAURYAN gap] ──▶ Guptas
North India : Shungas → Kanvas
Kalinga     : Chedis (Kharavela)
South       : Satavahanas
North-west  : Indo-Greeks → Shakas → Parthians → Kushanas
```

### Terms explained
- **Post-Mauryan period** — the time between the Mauryan fall and the Gupta rise.
- **Indo-Greeks** — Greek-descended rulers of the north-west, the first of the invading wave.

### Don't confuse
- **Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Parthians, Kushanas** (post-Mauryan invaders) are not the **Hunas/Turks** (much later invaders).

**Remember it:** Three post-Mauryan Indian dynasties = "SKC" — Shunga, Kanva, Chedi.

**TL;DR**
- Post-Mauryan = gap between the Mauryas and the Guptas (2nd c. BCE – 3rd c. AD).
- Indian dynasties: Shungas, Kanvas, Chedis; Satavahanas in the south.
- North-west invaders in order: Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Parthians, Kushanas.
keyPoints: Post-Mauryan period spans the 2nd century BCE to 3rd century AD — between the Mauryan fall and the Gupta rise.
The Mauryan Empire disintegrated after Ashoka's death because of weak successors and provinces breaking away.
Regional powers emerged: Shungas, Kanvas, Chedis; Satavahanas took the south and Kalinga became independent.
Central Asian tribes — Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Parthians, Kushanas — invaded the north-west.
The Shungas were Brahmanical rulers who reacted against Mauryan Buddhist policy.
items.mnemonic: Three post-Mauryan Indian dynasties = 'SKC' → Shunga → Kanva → Chedi.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan (Post-Mauryan Period; Political Developments)

items.title: Pushyamitra Shunga & the Founding of the Shunga Dynasty
items.body:
## Pushyamitra Shunga & the Founding of the Shunga Dynasty

**In one line:** Pushyamitra Shunga, a Mauryan general, killed the last Mauryan king and founded the Shunga dynasty in 185 BCE, defending north India and reviving Brahmanical rituals.

**Why it is asked:** The founder, the year (185 BCE), the two Ashvamedha sacrifices and the Shunga capitals are high-frequency single-fact questions.

### The story
- **Cause:** as the Mauryan Empire weakened, its own army commander saw his chance.
- **Event:** **Pushyamitra Shunga**, a **general of the Mauryas**, **assassinated the last Mauryan king Brihadratha** and set up the **Shunga dynasty** in **185 BCE**, with capitals at **Pataliputra and Vidisha** and territory reaching **central and northern India up to the Narmada River**.
- **Result:** he **resisted Indo-Greek invasions** and the raids of **Kharavela of Kalinga**, protecting the **Gangetic Valley**, and performed **two Ashvamedha Yagnas** (recorded in the **Ayodhya Inscription**) to proclaim his sovereignty.
- Though a **Brahmanist**, he **renovated the Bharhut Stupa**; he is also named in **Banabhatta's Harshacharita**.

### Picture it
| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Founder | Pushyamitra Shunga (Mauryan general) |
| Year / span | 185 BCE; dynasty 185–73 BCE |
| Capitals | Pataliputra and Vidisha |
| Legitimacy | Two Ashvamedha Yagnas (Ayodhya Inscription) |

### Terms explained
- **Ashvamedha Yagna** — the Vedic horse-sacrifice performed to proclaim a king's supreme sovereignty.
- **Ayodhya Inscription** — the record (of Dhanadeva) noting Pushyamitra's two horse-sacrifices.

### Don't confuse
- **Pushyamitra Shunga** founded the Shunga dynasty (185 BCE); **Vasudeva Kanva** later founded the Kanva dynasty (73 BCE) — different men, different dates.

**Remember it:** "P kills B" — Pushyamitra killed Brihadratha to start the Shungas.

**TL;DR**
- Pushyamitra Shunga, a Mauryan general, killed Brihadratha and founded the Shungas in 185 BCE.
- Capitals Pataliputra and Vidisha; territory up to the Narmada.
- Two Ashvamedha Yagnas (Ayodhya Inscription); resisted Indo-Greeks; renovated Bharhut Stupa.

figure.alt: Map of the Sunga Empire around 185 BCE showing territory up to the Narmada with Pataliputra, Vidisa, Bharhut and Saketa, bordered by the Greco-Bactrian and Satavahana realms
figure.caption: The Sunga Empire (c. 185 BCE) reached central-northern India up to the Narmada, with Pataliputra and Vidisa as centres and Bharhut within its territory.

keyPoints: Pushyamitra Shunga, a Mauryan general, killed the last Mauryan king Brihadratha and founded the Shunga dynasty in 185 BCE.
Shunga capitals were Pataliputra and Vidisha; territory extended to the Narmada River.
Pushyamitra performed two Ashvamedha Yagnas (Ayodhya Inscription) to assert legitimacy.
He resisted Indo-Greek invasions and Kharavela of Kalinga while protecting the Gangetic Valley.
Though a Brahmanist, he renovated the Bharhut Stupa; he is mentioned in Banabhatta's Harshacharita.
items.mnemonic: Pushyamitra 'PB': Pushyamitra killed Brihadratha — and did two aShvamedhas ('Shunga').
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan (Shunga Dynasty; Pushyamitra Shunga)

items.title: Key Rulers of the Shunga Dynasty
items.body:
## Key Rulers of the Shunga Dynasty

**In one line:** After Pushyamitra, Shunga rulers like Agnimitra, Vasumitra and Bhagabhadra are each remembered for one landmark — a play, a victory or a famous pillar — down to the last king Devabhuti.

**Why it is asked:** Ruler-to-association matching (Agnimitra–Malvikagnimitra, Bhagabhadra–Heliodorus Pillar) is a classic question format.

### The story
- **Agnimitra Shunga (149 BCE – 141 BCE)** — the hero of **Kalidasa's play Malvikagnimitra**, which tells of his romance with **Princess Malvika**; he **suppressed rebellions in Vidarbha**.
- **Vasumitra** — **defended the dynasty against Indo-Greek invasions**.
- **Bhagabhadra** — in his reign a **Greek ambassador** set up the **Heliodorus Pillar** near **Vidisha**, dedicated to **Vasudeva (Krishna)** — proof that even Greeks were drawn to Bhagavatism.
- **Devabhuti** — the **last Shunga ruler**, **assassinated by his minister Vasudeva Kanva**, which ended the dynasty.

### Picture it
| Ruler | Remembered for |
|---|---|
| Agnimitra | Kalidasa's Malvikagnimitra; Vidarbha revolt |
| Vasumitra | Defence against the Indo-Greeks |
| Bhagabhadra | Heliodorus Pillar, Vidisha |
| Devabhuti | Last Shunga; killed by Vasudeva Kanva |

### Terms explained
- **Heliodorus Pillar** — a pillar near Vidisha raised by the Greek envoy Heliodorus in honour of Vasudeva Krishna.
- **Bhagavatism** — early devotion to Vishnu/Krishna (Vasudeva).

### Don't confuse
- **Malvikagnimitra** (about Agnimitra) is by **Kalidasa**; the **Harshacharita** (which names Pushyamitra) is by **Banabhatta** — different works.

**Remember it:** The Heliodorus Pillar = a Greek bowing to Krishna, in Bhagabhadra's reign.

**TL;DR**
- Agnimitra (149–141 BCE): hero of Kalidasa's Malvikagnimitra; crushed the Vidarbha revolt.
- Vasumitra defended against the Indo-Greeks; Bhagabhadra is linked to the Heliodorus Pillar at Vidisha.
- Devabhuti, the last Shunga, was killed by Vasudeva Kanva.
keyPoints: Agnimitra (149–141 BCE) features in Kalidasa's Malvikagnimitra and suppressed Vidarbha rebellions.
Vasumitra defended the dynasty against Indo-Greek invasions.
Bhagabhadra is linked to the Heliodorus Pillar near Vidisha, dedicated by a Greek envoy to Vasudeva Krishna.
Devabhuti was the last Shunga ruler.
Devabhuti's assassination by Vasudeva Kanva ended the Shunga dynasty.
Agnimitra, son of Pushyamitra, is the hero of Kalidasa's play Malavikagnimitra.
items.mnemonic: Heliodorus Pillar = a Greek bowing to Krishna — foreign devotion to Vasudeva under Bhagabhadra.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan (Key Rulers of the Shunga Dynasty)

items.title: The Kanva Dynasty (73 BCE – 28 BCE)
items.body:
## The Kanva Dynasty (73 BCE – 28 BCE)

**In one line:** The Kanva dynasty began when a Brahmin Shunga minister, Vasudeva Kanva, killed the last Shunga king in 73 BCE, and it ended when the Satavahanas overthrew its last ruler.

**Why it is asked:** The founder-and-year (Vasudeva Kanva, 73 BCE), the Panchala coins of Bhumimitra, and "who ended the Kanvas" are repeat facts.

### The story
- **Cause:** the Shunga dynasty had weakened, and its own **Brahmin minister** seized the throne.
- **Event:** **Vasudeva Kanva killed Devabhuti** and founded the **Kanva dynasty** in **73 BCE**, ruling from **Pataliputra and Vidisha** and keeping the **Shunga administrative structure** for continuity.
- **Rulers:** **Bhumimitra** succeeded him — **coins bearing his name in the Panchala region** attest his control; **Narayana** struggled to hold power; **Susharman**, the **last Kanva ruler**, was **overthrown by the Satavahanas**, ending the line.
- The Kanvas upheld **Brahmanical traditions** and performed **Vedic rituals** across the Gangetic plain.

### Picture it
| Ruler | Note |
|---|---|
| Vasudeva Kanva | Founder (73 BCE); killed Devabhuti |
| Bhumimitra | Coins in Panchala |
| Narayana | Held power amid challenges |
| Susharman | Last; overthrown by Satavahanas |

### Terms explained
- **Panchala** — a region of the upper Gangetic plain where Bhumimitra's coins were found.
- **Satavahanas** — the southern dynasty that ended Kanva rule.

### Don't confuse
- **Vasudeva Kanva** (founder of the Kanvas) is not **Vasudeva Krishna** (the deity of the Heliodorus Pillar).

**Remember it:** Kanva line "VBNS" — Vasudeva, Bhumimitra, Narayana, Susharman (ends at the Satavahanas).

**TL;DR**
- Vasudeva Kanva, a Brahmin Shunga minister, killed Devabhuti and founded the Kanvas in 73 BCE.
- Bhumimitra's Panchala coins show his rule; capitals Pataliputra and Vidisha.
- The last Kanva, Susharman, was overthrown by the Satavahanas.

figure.alt: Map of India in the 1st century BCE showing Magadha under the Kanva Dynasty flanked by the Satavahana Empire, Indo-Scythian kingdoms and Kalinga
figure.caption: The Kanva dynasty ruled Magadha and the Gangetic plain, bordered by the Satavahanas to the south and Indo-Scythians to the north-west.

keyPoints: Vasudeva Kanva, a Brahmin Shunga minister, killed Devabhuti and founded the Kanva dynasty in 73 BCE.
Kanva capitals were Pataliputra and Vidisha; they upheld Brahmanical traditions and Vedic rituals.
Bhumimitra succeeded Vasudeva; coins of his found in Panchala show his control there.
Narayana struggled to hold power amid mounting challenges.
Susharman, the last Kanva ruler, was overthrown by the Satavahanas.
items.mnemonic: Kanva line 'VBNS' → Vasudeva → Bhumimitra → Narayana → Susharman (ends at Satavahanas).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan (Kanva Dynasty; Key Rulers of the Kanva Dynasty)

items.title: The Chedi (Mahameghavahana) Dynasty & Kharavela
items.body:
## The Chedi (Mahameghavahana) Dynasty & Kharavela

**In one line:** The Chedi dynasty of Kalinga, founded by Abhichandra, produced the Jain warrior-king Kharavela, whose deeds are recorded in the famous Hathigumpha inscription.

**Why it is asked:** Kharavela, the Hathigumpha inscription and the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves are among the most-tested post-Mauryan facts, and Kalinga is an AP-adjacent region.

### The story
- The **Chedi Dynasty**, also called the **Mahameghavahana Dynasty**, rose in **Kalinga** in the **1st century BCE** after Mauryan decline; it was **founded by King Abhichandra** with capital at **Suktimati-Puri** (on the Suktimati River).
- Its greatest ruler, **Kharavela**, was a **Jain king** famed for **military conquests** and **religious patronage**.
- His achievements are recorded in the **Hathigumpha Inscription (Brahmi script)** in the **Udayagiri hills**; he launched **campaigns against the Satavahanas** and **expanded Kalinga's territory**.
- He built the **Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves** as **homes for Jain monks**, and his son **Kudepasiri** is named in the **Mancapuri Cave Inscription**.

### Picture it
| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Dynasty | Chedi / Mahameghavahana of Kalinga |
| Founder / capital | Abhichandra / Suktimati-Puri |
| Greatest ruler | Kharavela (Jain) |
| Record | Hathigumpha Inscription (Brahmi, Udayagiri) |

### Terms explained
- **Hathigumpha** — "elephant cave", the Udayagiri cave bearing Kharavela's inscription.
- **Mahameghavahana** — the family/dynastic name of the Chedi rulers of Kalinga.

### Don't confuse
- **Abhichandra** founded the dynasty; **Kharavela** was its greatest ruler (not the founder); **Kudepasiri** was Kharavela's son.

**Remember it:** Kharavela = the Jain king of the "elephant cave" (Hathigumpha) in Kalinga.

**TL;DR**
- Chedi (Mahameghavahana) dynasty of Kalinga; founder Abhichandra, capital Suktimati-Puri.
- Kharavela, a Jain king, recorded in the Hathigumpha Inscription (Brahmi, Udayagiri).
- He campaigned against the Satavahanas and built the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves; son Kudepasiri (Mancapuri).
keyPoints: The Chedi (Mahameghavahana) dynasty rose in Kalinga; founded by Abhichandra with capital Suktimati-Puri.
Kharavela was a Jain ruler famed for conquests and religious patronage.
His deeds are recorded in the Hathigumpha Inscription (Brahmi script) in the Udayagiri hills.
He campaigned against the Satavahanas and built the Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves for Jain monks.
His son Kudepasiri appears in the Mancapuri Cave Inscription.
items.mnemonic: Kharavela = 'Jain King of the Elephant Cave' — Hathigumpha ('elephant cave') records his Kalinga deeds.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan (Chedi (Mahameghavahana) Dynasty; King Kharavela)

items.title: Stupas & Buddhist Architecture (Sanchi, Bharhut, Amaravati)
items.body:
## Stupas & Buddhist Architecture (Sanchi, Bharhut, Amaravati)

**In one line:** The post-Mauryan age enriched India's great Buddhist stupas — Sanchi, Bharhut and Amaravati — with carved gateways and narrative reliefs, even under the Brahmanical Shungas.

**Why it is asked:** Stupa-to-feature matching (Sanchi toranas, Bharhut-Cunningham, Amaravati marble) is one of the most common art-and-architecture questions.

### The story
- **Sanchi Stupa (Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh)** — originally built by **Ashoka** and **expanded by the Shungas**; famous for **elaborate toranas (gateways)** carved with **Jataka tales**; it stands on the **Dakshinapatha** trade route.
- **Bharhut Stupa (Satna, Madhya Pradesh)** — **discovered by Alexander Cunningham**; noted for **red stone railings** and **narrative reliefs** such as **Queen Mayadevi's dream** and the **Ruru Jataka**.
- **Amaravati Stupa (Andhra Pradesh)** — famed for **intricate white-marble carvings**, **Buddhist narratives**, **floral motifs** and **scenes from the Buddha's life**.
- Although the **Shungas** promoted Brahmanism, they **renovated Buddhist monuments** and introduced **decorated toranas**; the **Kanvas** continued Brahmanical temple construction in the same tradition.

### Picture it
| Stupa | Feature |
|---|---|
| Sanchi | Ashoka-built, Shunga-expanded; toranas; Dakshinapatha |
| Bharhut | Cunningham; red railings; Mayadevi's dream, Ruru Jataka |
| Amaravati | White marble; Buddha's life, floral motifs |

### Terms explained
- **Stupa** — a dome-shaped Buddhist monument built over sacred relics.
- **Torana** — the ornately carved gateway of a stupa.
- **Jataka tales** — stories of the Buddha's previous births, carved on stupa railings.

### Don't confuse
- **Alexander Cunningham** discovered the **Bharhut** stupa (not Sanchi); do not swap the two.

**Remember it:** Stupa trio "SBA" — Sanchi (toranas), Bharhut (Cunningham, red railings), Amaravati (marble narratives).

**TL;DR**
- Sanchi: Ashokan origin, Shunga expansion, toranas with Jataka tales, on the Dakshinapatha.
- Bharhut: discovered by Cunningham; red railings; Mayadevi's dream and Ruru Jataka reliefs.
- Amaravati (AP): white-marble carvings of the Buddha's life; Shungas renovated Buddhist stupas despite Brahmanism.

figure.alt: The Great Stupa at Sanchi with its hemispherical dome, railing and elaborately carved torana gateway against a blue sky
figure.caption: The Great Stupa at Sanchi — begun by Ashoka and expanded by the Shungas, famous for its carved toranas depicting Jataka tales.

keyPoints: Sanchi Stupa (Vidisha) was begun by Ashoka and expanded by the Shungas; known for toranas and Jataka scenes on the Dakshinapatha route.
Bharhut Stupa (Satna) was discovered by Alexander Cunningham; noted for red stone railings and reliefs of Mayadevi's dream and the Ruru Jataka.
Amaravati Stupa (Andhra Pradesh) is known for intricate carvings, floral motifs and scenes from the Buddha's life.
The Shungas renovated Buddhist stupas and introduced decorated toranas despite promoting Brahmanism.
The Kanvas continued Brahmanical temple construction in the Shunga artistic tradition.
items.mnemonic: Stupa trio 'SBA' → Sanchi (toranas) · Bharhut (Cunningham, red railings) · Amaravati (marble narratives).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan (Art and Architecture; Stupas; Contribution of Various Dynasties)

items.title: Rock-cut Architecture & Schools of Sculpture
items.body:
## Rock-cut Architecture & Schools of Sculpture

**In one line:** The period produced Jain rock-cut caves in Odisha and the three great sculpture schools — Mathura, Gandhara and Amaravati — each recognised by its distinctive stone.

**Why it is asked:** School-to-material matching (Mathura red sandstone, Gandhara grey schist, Amaravati white marble) is a guaranteed-type question.

### The story
- **Rock-cut architecture:** the **Udayagiri and Khandagiri Caves (Odisha)**, built under **Kharavela**, hold the **Hathigumpha inscription** and the double-storey **Ranigumpha Cave**; the **Ajanta Caves (Maharashtra)** evolved from simple **Hinayana** caves to painted **Mahayana** caves with **Jataka tales** and royal processions.
- **Schools of sculpture:**
  - **Mathura School (Uttar Pradesh)** — **red sandstone**; early **Buddha statues** and **Jain Tirthankara** images with stylised indigenous features.
  - **Gandhara School (north-west India / Pakistan)** — **grey schist**; **Greco-Roman realism** with **Greek-style drapery and curly hair**.
  - **Amaravati School (Andhra Pradesh)** — **white marble**; detailed Buddhist narratives and floral motifs.

### Picture it
| School | Stone | Hallmark |
|---|---|---|
| Mathura | Red sandstone | Indigenous Buddha and Jain images |
| Gandhara | Grey schist | Greco-Roman realism, curly hair |
| Amaravati | White marble | Buddhist narratives, floral motifs |

### Terms explained
- **Schist** — a grey layered rock used by the Gandhara sculptors.
- **Hinayana / Mahayana** — the earlier (no Buddha image) and later (Buddha image) phases of Buddhism, seen in Ajanta's two cave groups.

### Don't confuse
- **Mathura** = red sandstone (indigenous); **Gandhara** = grey schist (Greek-influenced); **Amaravati** = white marble.

**Remember it:** Sculpture stones "R-G-W" — Mathura Red sandstone, Gandhara Grey schist, Amaravati White marble.

**TL;DR**
- Udayagiri-Khandagiri (Kharavela) and Ajanta (Hinayana to Mahayana) are the key rock-cut sites.
- Mathura = red sandstone; Gandhara = grey schist (Greco-Roman); Amaravati = white marble.
- Gandhara shows Greek drapery and curly hair; Amaravati (AP) favours narrative panels.
keyPoints: Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves (Odisha) were built under Kharavela and hold the Hathigumpha inscription and the double-storey Ranigumpha cave.
Ajanta caves (Maharashtra) progress from simple Hinayana to Mahayana caves with Buddha sculptures and Jataka paintings.
Mathura School used red sandstone for early Buddha and Jain Tirthankara images.
Gandhara School used grey schist and Greco-Roman influence for realistic Buddhas with Greek drapery and curly hair.
Amaravati School used white marble for detailed Buddhist narratives and floral motifs.
items.mnemonic: Sculpture stones: Mathura = red sandstone, Gandhara = grey schist, Amaravati = white marble (R-G-W).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan (Rock-cut Architecture; Schools of Sculpture)

items.title: Patanjali, the Mahabhashya & Language
items.body:
## Patanjali, the Mahabhashya & Language

**In one line:** Sanskrit revived in the post-Mauryan age, and the grammarian Patanjali — linked to Pushyamitra's court — wrote the Mahabhashya and the Yoga Sutras.

**Why it is asked:** "Patanjali's two works" and the Panini–Patanjali link are repeat questions, often with a trap option (Ashtadhyayi is Panini's, not Patanjali's).

### The story
- **Sanskrit gained prominence**, becoming the language of **religious and literary texts**.
- **Patanjali** authored the **Mahabhashya**, a great commentary on **Sanskrit grammar** (specifically on Panini's rules), and the **Yoga Sutras** on **yoga philosophy**; he is traditionally linked to the Shunga court of **Pushyamitra**.
- The **Brahmi script** evolved further, connected to the **Kalinga Brahmi** and **Maurya scripts** — the same Brahmi used for Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription.

### Picture it
| Work | Subject |
|---|---|
| Mahabhashya | Commentary on Sanskrit grammar |
| Yoga Sutras | Yoga philosophy |

### Terms explained
- **Mahabhashya** — Patanjali's "great commentary" on Panini's grammar.
- **Ashtadhyayi** — Panini's grammar book (not Patanjali's); Patanjali's Mahabhashya comments on it.

### Don't confuse
- **Panini** wrote the **Ashtadhyayi**; **Patanjali** wrote the **Mahabhashya** that comments on it — do not swap author and work.

**Remember it:** Patanjali's pair = "grammar + yoga" — Mahabhashya (language) and Yoga Sutras (mind).

**TL;DR**
- Sanskrit became the leading literary language in the post-Mauryan age.
- Patanjali, linked to Pushyamitra's court, wrote the Mahabhashya (grammar) and the Yoga Sutras (yoga).
- Brahmi script evolved further; the Ashtadhyayi is Panini's, not Patanjali's.
keyPoints: Sanskrit became the dominant language of religious and literary texts in the post-Mauryan period.
Patanjali authored the Mahabhashya on Sanskrit grammar.
Patanjali also wrote the Yoga Sutras on yoga philosophy.
The Brahmi script evolved further, connected to the Kalinga Brahmi and Maurya scripts.
Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription is itself in the Brahmi script.
items.mnemonic: Patanjali = two great works — 'grammar + yoga' → Mahabhashya (language) and Yoga Sutras (mind).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan (Language and Literature)

items.title: Religion & Society in the Post-Mauryan Period
items.body:
## Religion & Society in the Post-Mauryan Period

**In one line:** Under the Shungas, Brahmanism revived — Vedic sacrifices returned and the Varna system hardened, while the Manusmriti narrowed women's roles.

**Why it is asked:** The Brahmanical revival, the rigid Varna order and the Manusmriti's rules on women are common statement-type questions.

### The story
- **Cause:** the Shungas, as Brahmanists, reacted against Mauryan Buddhist policy.
- **What happened:** **Brahmanism regained prominence**, reviving **Vedic rituals** such as the **Ashvamedha Yagna**; the **Varna system became rigid**, with **priests and rulers dominating** and **Shudras facing discrimination**.
- **Result:** **women's roles were restricted to domestic duties**, as prescribed in the **Manusmriti**, even as **mixed castes emerged** when foreigners (Greeks, Shakas and others) integrated into Indian society.

### Picture it
| Area | Change under the Shungas |
|---|---|
| Religion | Vedic rituals revived (Ashvamedha) |
| Caste | Varna system becomes rigid |
| Women | Domestic roles (Manusmriti) |
| Foreigners | Absorbed as mixed castes |

### Terms explained
- **Varna system** — the fourfold ordering of society (Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra).
- **Manusmriti** — an ancient law text that prescribed social and gender duties.

### Don't confuse
- The **Shungas revived Brahmanism**, but they did not persecute all Buddhists — they even renovated Buddhist stupas like Bharhut.

**Remember it:** Shunga society = "rigid Varna + Manusmriti" — a Brahmanical revival that hardened the hierarchy.

**TL;DR**
- Brahmanism revived under the Shungas; Vedic rituals like the Ashvamedha returned.
- The Varna system became rigid; Shudras faced discrimination.
- The Manusmriti restricted women to domestic roles; foreigners were absorbed as mixed castes.
keyPoints: Brahmanism revived under the Shungas, reviving Vedic rituals such as the Ashvamedha Yagna.
The Varna system became rigid, reinforcing social hierarchy.
Priests and rulers dominated society while Shudras faced continued discrimination.
Women's roles were restricted to domestic duties as prescribed in the Manusmriti.
Mixed castes emerged as foreigners integrated into Indian society.

items.title: Trade & Commerce in the Post-Mauryan Period
items.body:
## Trade & Commerce in the Post-Mauryan Period

**In one line:** Post-Mauryan trade boomed through merchant guilds, the great overland routes Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha, and monsoon-driven sea trade with Rome.

**Why it is asked:** The two named trade routes, Mathura's shataka cloth and the monsoon-wind Roman trade are frequent factual questions.

### The story
- **Merchant guilds and trading corporations** flourished, organising craft and commerce.
- **Mathura** became known for producing **shataka cloth**.
- The **Uttarapatha** (northern route) and **Dakshinapatha** (southern route) were the **major overland trade routes** linking different regions of the subcontinent.
- **Monsoon winds facilitated maritime trade** with **Rome and Southeast Asia**, so Indian goods reached distant overseas markets.

### Picture it
| Element | Detail |
|---|---|
| Organisation | Merchant guilds / corporations |
| Famous good | Mathura's shataka cloth |
| Overland routes | Uttarapatha (north), Dakshinapatha (south) |
| Sea trade | Monsoon winds to Rome and Southeast Asia |

### Terms explained
- **Guild** — an association of merchants or craftsmen regulating a trade.
- **Uttarapatha / Dakshinapatha** — the great northern and southern highways of ancient India.

### Don't confuse
- **Uttarapatha** is the northern route; **Dakshinapatha** is the southern route (Dakshina = south).

**Remember it:** Two great routes = "U and D" — Uttarapatha (north) and Dakshinapatha (south).

**TL;DR**
- Merchant guilds and corporations drove post-Mauryan commerce.
- Mathura produced shataka cloth; Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha were the main overland routes.
- Monsoon winds carried maritime trade to Rome and Southeast Asia.
keyPoints: Merchant guilds and trading corporations flourished in the post-Mauryan economy.
Mathura was famous for producing shataka cloth.
Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha were the two major trade routes.
Monsoon winds enabled maritime trade with Rome and Southeast Asia.
Growing commerce linked the subcontinent to distant overseas markets.

items.title: For Mains — Post-Mauryan: Sungas, Kanvas & Chedis
items.body:
## For Mains — Post-Mauryan: Sungas, Kanvas & Chedis

**In one line:** For Mains (GS Paper-2, clause M2-1b: Satavahanas, Sangam, Sungas, Guptas), the post-Mauryan dynasties are examined as a bridge age — political continuity, Brahmanical and Jain revival, and a flowering of narrative art.

### Dimensions Mains asks
| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Political role | Shungas held north India and repelled Indo-Greeks; Kanvas continued; Chedis revived Kalinga |
| Religion/society | Brahmanical revival (Ashvamedha, rigid Varna, Manusmriti) alongside Jain (Kharavela) and Buddhist patronage |
| Art & architecture | Sanchi/Bharhut/Amaravati stupas; toranas; Mathura/Gandhara/Amaravati sculpture schools |
| Significance | Preserved continuity between the Mauryas and Guptas; set the stage for classical art |
| Criticism/limits | Fragmented, short-lived dynasties; founded by assassination; rigid social order |

### Data points / authorities to quote
- **Hathigumpha Inscription** (Brahmi, Udayagiri) — the chief record of Kharavela of Kalinga.
- **Ayodhya Inscription** — Pushyamitra's two Ashvamedha Yagnas.
- **Heliodorus Pillar (Besnagar, Vidisha)** — a Greek envoy honouring Vasudeva Krishna under Bhagabhadra.
- **Kalidasa's Malvikagnimitra** — literary window on Agnimitra Shunga.
- **Alexander Cunningham** — rediscovery of the Bharhut Stupa.

### The AP angle
- The **Amaravati Stupa and Amaravati School of sculpture (white marble, Krishna/Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh)** belong to this age and flowered under the neighbouring **Satavahanas** — a strong AP hook for any art-and-architecture answer; Kalinga's Kharavela also campaigned toward the Andhra Satavahanas.

### Use in answers
- **Example:** cite the Amaravati School (AP) to localise post-Mauryan art.
- **Quote:** note the Heliodorus Pillar as evidence of Greeks embracing Bhagavatism.
- **Diagram idea:** a timeline bar "Mauryas → Shungas (185 BCE) → Kanvas (73 BCE) → Satavahanas"; or a stupa-feature table.
keyPoints: Mains clause M2-1b (GS Paper-2): Sungas among Satavahanas/Sangam/Guptas — treat as a bridge age, analytically.
Angles: political continuity and defence of north India, Brahmanical/Jain/Buddhist patronage, flowering of narrative art.
Quote evidence: Hathigumpha and Ayodhya inscriptions, Heliodorus Pillar, Kalidasa's Malvikagnimitra, Cunningham on Bharhut.
AP angle: the Amaravati Stupa and Amaravati sculpture school (white marble, Andhra) belong to this age under the Satavahanas.
Balance: these were fragmented, short-lived dynasties founded by assassination, with a hardened social order.
Use a Mauryas → Shungas → Kanvas → Satavahanas timeline and a stupa-feature table in answers.
